post.text:
Single biggest improvement I made to my CLAUDE.md:

"When I report a bug, don't start by trying to fix it. Instead, start by writing a test that reproduces the bug. Then, have subagents try to fix the bug and prove it with a passing test."

1/ Most developers (and AI agents) see a bug and immediately start hacking at the code.

That's backwards.

You're guessing at the fix before you even understand the failure.

2/ Here's what happens when you let Claude Code jump straight to fixing:

- It changes 3 files
- The bug looks fixed
- You ship it
- A week later the same bug is back, slightly different

Sound familiar?

3/ The test-first approach forces a different workflow:

Step 1: Write a test that fails exactly the way the bug fails
Step 2: Now you have a precise definition of the problem
Step 3: Subagents work on fixes in parallel
Step 4: The fix isn't done until the test passes

4/ Why subagents?

Because once you have a failing test, the fix becomes an embarrassingly parallel problem.

Spin up 3 subagents. Each tries a different approach. The one that makes the test green wins.

No more serial guess-and-check.

5/ The failing test also acts as a guard rail.

Subagents can't claim they fixed it. The test either passes or it doesn't. No hand-waving. No "I think this should work."

6/ Add this to your CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md today:

"When I report a bug, don't start by trying to fix it. Instead, start by writing a test that reproduces the bug. Then, have subagents try to fix the bug and prove it with a passing test."

One sentence. Massive behavior change.

7/ This works because it shifts the AI from "creative problem solver" mode to "engineer who writes proof" mode.

The constraint of a failing test eliminates the most common failure mode: fixing the wrong thing.
